html:
The Tamaulipecos were the many small bands of hunters and gatherers who lived in what is now Tamaulipas, in northeastern Mexico, when the Spanish arrived. Little is known about them beyond Spanish records.

They lived in the dry plains, hills and coastal lagoons between the Gulf of Mexico and the Sierra Madre Oriental, moving with the seasons for game, fish, roots and cactus fruit. The Spanish counted dozens of named groups and grouped them loosely with the Coahuiltecan peoples to the north.

The region stayed outside Spanish control for two centuries. In 1748 José de Escandón founded the colony of Nuevo Santander for New Spain and settled ranchers and missions there. War, disease and mixing with settlers followed, and by the 1800s the Tamaulipeco bands had disappeared as separate peoples.
